sourceInformation.source: The Wire (2002-2008), created by David Simon and Ed Burns
sourceInformation.perspective: Third-person 3/4 camera on the Corner (V cycles to the side view); side view in the Wire Room
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge v0.85.1 engine (handoff package, one file, no dependencies); AI Hub Session Protocol v1, client 1.3.0
sourceInformation.artDirection: Engine-native pixel art on a PS1-style low-resolution buffer: brick rowhouses, a stash-house roof, streetlamps, dusk lighting
sourceInformation.animation: Engine-native skeletal rigs (E.Humanoid), telegraphed attacks (E.Attack), takedown and parry actions
sourceInformation.audio: All code-written: chip-style songs in layers for the Corner and the Wire Room, synth sound effects, and Animalese-style gibberish voices pitched per speaker
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub parallel mode (1-4 players, each on their own copy, scored on time). No other network use
sourceInformation.testing: Headless Chromium (Playwright) for the flow, scoring and screens, the WebKit phone profiles via viewport-matrix, and the AI Hub harness for multiplayer (2 players, and 4 with latency, jitter and loss)
sourceInformation.research: Read the engine handoff docs (API card, kits README, the stealth kit source) and the AI Hub session protocol README
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux; browser unknown

testingFeedback: Ten issues: five found by reading the code before the first run, five by the browser runs (a glyph that rendered as a question mark, a line that could not be flagged until its typing finished, the About screen opening over an open results panel, the touch-only title still showing the keyboard hint, and the mouse click mapping in the new Wire Room code, which the mouse test caught). One harness failure was not the game's: another agent's server held the port the harness used.
One critical issue, caught in review before any run: the Wire Room would have thrown on entry, because its helper was scoped inside the Corner. It was fixed; no player would have reached it.

The most helpful test was the AI Hub harness: it names every protocol check, and it passed for 2 players and for 4 players with latency, jitter and packet loss. A close second: a fake standard-mapping gamepad injected into the page, which proved the stick inversion (normal [0.8, -0.6], inverted [-0.8, 0.6]).

The least helpful test was the timed screenshot wait for attract mode: it took twelve seconds to show what the code already covered, and the Settings screenshot missed the Controller group until a DOM check.
engineFeedback: The stealth kit was the best part: guards with sight cones, takedowns and parries, and a HUD in one readable file. The Shell's results and settings screens, and the E.Dialog choices, worked without extra code.

I guessed on the stick inversion, since the settings screen has no axis option: I defined the toggles and wrapped the input in a proxy that inverts only pad sticks, then checked it with a simulated pad. I guessed the guards' weapon name and used 'sword', because the API card has no list of weapon names. game.screen.clientToScreen returned (0.33, 0) for the canvas centre in my test, so I mapped pointers from the canvas rectangle myself. E.Shell screens also stay open across scene changes, so the About screen opened over the results panel until I closed it by hand.

The most important things I built myself: the Wire Room minigame, the Animalese voices (a blip per letter, pitched per speaker), the scrolling About screen with the feedback text, the attract-mode route, and the AI Hub round glue.

The hardest part was the size: a 1.2 MB single file and a 66 KB API card. I read the stealth kit closely to learn the patterns, and a full clone of the repository filled the temporary disk, so I had to fetch only the handoff folder.
I would overhaul the Shell's screen lifetime: a screen should close when its scene changes, or the scene should be able to close it with one call.
I would add a built-in stick-inversion option to the Controller settings group, and a short list of the rig's weapon names in the API card.
promptFeedback: The done criteria and the exit-interview shape were precise, and the links to the engine and hub README let me work from the real protocol rather than a guess.

The folder rules were unclear: the brief says to create the subfolder 'here' and to bundle the HTML 'in root', and I read 'root' as the work folder, where I put the HTML and the JSON. The brainstorm line says 50 titles and I produced 52. The Usage field asks for cost and token estimates that I could not measure.

The hardest thing was fitting the whole list into one pass: the controller-first UI with glyph swaps, attract mode, touch-only handling, the Wire Room with mouse and keyboard, the multiplayer round, and the test tools. I tested the pad with a simulated controller, not a real one, and I did not test on real iOS Safari.
The test I would most like to run is a real DualSense in Chrome, to confirm that the two inversion toggles and the glyph swap feel right, followed by a four-player round across separate machines.

aiHub.name: Wireframe Hour
aiHub.tagline: Stealth on the Corner. Listening in the Wire Room.
aiHub.description: A three-day Baltimore demo: steal a notebook off a stash-house roof past the corner boys, then flag the real lines in the wire room. Animalese voices, a choice that follows you, and a short timed round on the hub.
aiHub.controls: Stick or arrows move, Space jump, J strike, K block, C crouch, Shift sprint, L roll
